issues.legal_issue: A subsequent transferee who paid value in good faith and without notice of an earlier agreement to sell is protected from specific performance of that agreement.
material_facts: The owner agreed to sell the property to the claimant, and the time for completing the sale was later extended.
Before the extended deadline, the owner sold the property in separate transactions, and the later purchaser acquired the entire interest for value.
The evidence supported the finding that the owner was in financial need and sold in separate transactions for less than the price agreed with the claimant.
The purchaser’s father and guardian had occupied the property as a tenant before the purchase, with that account supported by evidence of an earlier usufructuary mortgage and possession.
The claimant’s evidence that the purchaser or his guardian knew of the earlier agreement was found unreliable, and the guardian’s denial of knowledge was not challenged in cross-examination.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the subsequent purchaser was a purchaser for value without notice was supported by the evidence and was not set aside. Specific performance could therefore not be enforced against that purchaser. The appeal was dismissed, subject to the purchaser’s voluntary additional payment to the claimant in full and final satisfaction of the damages claim, in addition to the damages already decreed against the original seller.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits specific performance against a person claiming under a contracting party by a later title, except a transferee for value who paid in good faith and without notice of the original contract. The subsequent transferee initially bears the burden of proving the exception: Bhup Narain Singh v. Gokul Chand Mahraj, AIR 1934 PC 68. Knowledge of facts that would put a transferee on inquiry, where an inquiry would disclose the earlier agreement, amounts to notice: Mohammad Aslam Khan v. Neraze Shah, AIR 1932 PC 228. Once both sides have led evidence, the dispute is decided on the evidence as a whole. Dr. Govindas v. Smt. Shantibai, AIR 1972 SC 1520, was distinguished as depending on its own circumstances.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and purchaser_paid_value and seller_resold_in_parts_under_financial_pressure and occupancy_as_tenant_preceded_purchase and no_credible_evidence_of_notice

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim for specific performance of an earlier agreement to sell against a later transferee.
predicates.purchaser_paid_value: The later purchaser paid consideration to acquire the property.
predicates.seller_resold_in_parts_under_financial_p: The seller resold the property in separate transactions while under financial pressure, for less than the amount agreed with the earlier claimant.
predicates.occupancy_as_tenant_preceded_purchase: The purchaser or the purchaser’s representative had occupied the property as a tenant before the purchase.
predicates.no_credible_evidence_of_notice: The evidence did not credibly establish that the purchaser or the purchaser’s representative knew of the earlier agreement or of facts that would lead an inquiry to disclose it.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns specific performance against a later purchaser who paid value, the seller resold in parts under financial pressure, prior tenancy explains the purchaser’s connection with the property, and credible evidence of notice is absent, the later purchaser is protected from specific performance.
